timeline: Khwarazm, on the far northern edge of the empire. An old general who has served three rulers is still alive. Somewhere on the road from the sultan's court, a secret order is travelling toward him. Its purpose is to have him killed.

Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Seven. Today's story is about an old general who served three rulers faithfully, and about the day his own sultan signed a secret order to have him killed.
The order failed. And what the old general did next is the reason Beyhaqi remembered him.
His name was Altuntash. In Turkish, the name means something like golden stone.
Like many of the great commanders of Ghazni, Altuntash did not begin life as a lord. He began as a slave soldier. In this world, that was not the end of a career. It was often the beginning.
Young Turks from the steppe were bought, trained as soldiers, and the best of them could rise to command armies and govern provinces.

Altuntash served Sebuktegin, the founder of the dynasty. Then he served Sebuktegin's son, the great Mahmud of Ghazni. He fought the Turkish kings who came down from beyond the Oxus river. He governed the city of Herat.
And in the year ten seventeen, when Mahmud conquered the rich land of Khwarazm, far to the north, on the lower Oxus near the Aral Sea, he gave it to Altuntash to rule.
From then on, Altuntash carried an old and proud title. Khwarazmshah. The king of Khwarazm.
For years he guarded that frontier. He kept the wild horsemen of the steppe from raiding the farms and the towns. He was far from the court, rich, respected and, above all, trusted.
Then, in the year ten thirty, Mahmud died.

You know what happened next, if you heard our earlier folios. Mahmud's two sons, Muhammad and Masud, fought over the throne. Masud won. His brother was blinded and locked away. And the new sultan began to sort the men he had inherited from his father.
Some of them he kept. Some he destroyed. In Folio One, we watched the old vizier Hasanak climb a gallows. Other great men of Mahmud's time were arrested, one after another.

Now put yourself in Altuntash's place, far away in Khwarazm. He is old. He has an army. He has money. He served the father, not the son. And every month, news arrives of another old servant of Mahmud who has fallen.
And put yourself in Masud's place. A powerful general sits on the northern edge of the empire, with his own army, his own treasury, and a famous old title. He is loyal, people say. But is he?
This is the kind of fear that grows in the dark. And at Masud's court, there was a man who knew how to water it.
His name will be familiar. Bu Sahl Zawzani.

In Folio Five, we met him as the clever, bitter rival of Beyhaqi's teacher, Bu Nasr Moshkan. In Folio Six, we heard him write a poem in praise of the sultan's lion hunt. Bu Sahl was close to Masud, and he had a gift for telling the sultan what the sultan half wanted to hear.
Beyhaqi gives a whole section of his book a title that says it plainly. Bu Sahl's mischief in the matter of Altuntash.
Bu Sahl pressed the idea that Altuntash could not be trusted. That he was too strong, too far away, too independent. That it would be wiser to remove him before he became a problem.
And Masud listened.
A secret order was sent to Khwarazm, to a commander there named Qaid Malanjuq. Its purpose was to have Altuntash killed.
Stop for a moment and think about that. Not a trial. Not a summons to court. A quiet death, arranged from far away, for a man who had served the dynasty for most of his life.
It did not work.

The secret did not stay secret, and the plot fell apart. The next section of Beyhaqi's book has a short and grim title. The killing of Qaid Malanjuq. The man who was meant to strike the blow did not survive it. Altuntash was alive, and he knew.
Now we come to the dangerous moment. An old general with an army has just learned that his sultan tried to murder him. What would you expect him to do?
Break away, perhaps. Declare Khwarazm his own. Make an alliance with the Turkish kings across the river, the enemies of Ghazni. Many men in his place would have done exactly that.
And at court, they knew it. Historians who have studied these events agree on the fear that now ran through Masud's circle. If Altuntash rebelled, the whole northern frontier could be lost.
So Masud did two things.

First, he turned on the man who had given him the idea. Bu Sahl Zawzani fell from favour. He was arrested, and his wealth and his servants were taken from him. It would not last forever. Bu Sahl was a survivor, and in time he came back. But for a while, the clever courtier paid for his cleverness.
Second, Masud wrote to Altuntash.

Beyhaqi preserves the letter in his book. That is one of the great treasures of this history. Beyhaqi worked in the royal chancery, the office where the sultan's letters were written, and he copied real documents into his story. So we are not reading a historian's guess about what the sultan said.
We are reading what the court actually sent.

Its purpose is clear. It was meant to calm an old servant of the state and to win back his trust. It is the sound of a powerful man trying very hard to undo a mistake, without ever quite saying the word mistake.
And Altuntash?
He did not rebel.
He stayed in Khwarazm. He kept his title. And he went on serving the sultan who had tried to have him killed.

We should be honest here. We cannot see inside his heart. Perhaps it was pure loyalty to the house he had served since he was a young man. Perhaps it was cool good sense. He was old, and a rebellion is a young man's gamble. Perhaps it was both. Beyhaqi lets his actions speak, and so will I.
Because the real test was still coming.

In the year ten thirty two, Masud decided to strike at Ali Tegin, a Turkish king who ruled beyond the Oxus, in the lands around Bukhara and Samarkand. Ali Tegin had long been a thorn in Ghazni's side. Masud made an alliance with another Turkish ruler against him. And he ordered the army of Khwarazm to march.
He ordered Altuntash.
Think of it. The same sultan who had sent a secret death sentence now sent an order to go to war for him. And the old general went.

Altuntash crossed into the lands beyond the river and met Ali Tegin's army at a place called Dabusiyya, on the road between Bukhara and Samarkand. Beyhaqi gives a whole section of his history to the planning of this war.
The battle was hard, and it decided nothing. Neither side broke the other. But Altuntash was badly wounded.
He did not lose his army. He held it together, and pulled it back out of danger. But the wound was mortal. Not long afterwards, Altuntash, Khwarazmshah, died.
He died in the service of the man who had tried to kill him.
Now a new figure steps forward. Remember his name, because he will matter a great deal in the folios to come.
Altuntash had a chief minister, his steward and right hand, a man from Shiraz named Ahmad, son of Abd al Samad.

An army far from home, whose commander is dying or dead, is in terrible danger. If the enemy learns of it, they attack. If the soldiers learn of it, they may scatter. It is said that Ahmad kept his master's death quiet until the army was safe.
What we know for certain is that he made peace with Ali Tegin, and that he brought the army home.
It was a quiet piece of work, done with a cool head and no glory. And the sultan noticed.

Not long afterwards, Masud needed a new vizier, the chief minister of the whole empire. Beyhaqi tells us whom he chose. Khwaja Ahmad, son of Abd al Samad. The steward of Khwarazm became the first minister of Ghazni. He would stand beside Masud through the hard years ahead.
And in Khwarazm, Altuntash's son Harun took charge of his father's land. But that is a story for another day.
Let me jump forward eight years, to show you why this story stayed with Beyhaqi.
By the year ten forty, everything was falling apart. The new enemies we will meet next week were winning. Masud was stubborn, suspicious, and listening to the wrong people again.

In one scene from those last days, Beyhaqi shows us the vizier speaking privately to none other than Bu Sahl Zawzani. That vizier was Ahmad, the old steward of Altuntash. And he says a sentence that Beyhaqi wrote down.
In Persian, it is very short.
In soltan na an ast ke bud.
This sultan is not the man he was.

I find it hard to hear that line without thinking of the old general who died at Dabusiyya. Ahmad had seen, with his own eyes, what loyalty looked like. He had seen a man stay faithful to a master who did not deserve it. And now, years later, he was watching that same master lose his way.
So what does Beyhaqi want us to take from Altuntash?
He does not preach. He shows. On one side, a sultan who listened to a whisper, and signed a secret order in the dark. On the other, an old servant who had every reason to betray him, and did not.

And between them, Bu Sahl, the man who whispered. Notice that Beyhaqi, who disliked him, does not invent anything to blacken his name. He simply sets down what Bu Sahl advised, and what it cost. That is enough.

In Beyhaqi's world, power is fragile. It does not depend only on armies and treasure. It depends on trust. And trust, once a king throws it away, is very hard to buy back, even with a beautiful letter.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: a ruler who listens to whispers against his most loyal men will one day find that he has none left.
